# Why Reproducible Research {#sec-why}

In 2006 a group at Duke University reported that gene-expression
signatures derived from cancer cell lines could predict which
patients would respond to which chemotherapy, and within a few
years three clinical trials were using those signatures to choose
patients' treatment. Two biostatisticians at the MD Anderson
Cancer Center, Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes, tried to
reproduce the analyses from the published data and could not.
When they reconstructed what must have been done, they found gene
lists offset by one row and the labels of sensitive and resistant
cell lines reversed [@baggerly2009deriving]. None of these errors
stopped any code from running, and each produced a signature that
looked like a finding. The trials were halted in 2010 and the
papers retracted [@iom2012omics]; what exposed the errors was not
peer review but months of forensic reconstruction that a
reproducible analysis would have made unnecessary.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*An article about computational science in a scientific
publication is not the scholarship itself, it is merely
advertising of the scholarship. The actual scholarship is
the complete software development environment and the
complete set of instructions which generated the figures.*

[Jonathan B. Buckheit and David L. Donoho]{.smallcaps},
*WaveLab and Reproducible Research* (1995)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

## What 'reproducible' means {#sec-why-meaning}

Reproducibility is the lowest bar a scientific analysis must
clear. It says nothing about whether the analysis is correct,
important, or even sensible. It says only that a second analyst,
given the same inputs, can obtain the same outputs. Published
analyses nonetheless fail this bar often, when someone outside
the original team tries to rerun them from the materials
provided.

The terms in this space are slippery. The most useful taxonomy is
that of Goodman, Fanelli, and Ioannidis [-@goodman2016what], which
distinguishes three kinds by what is held fixed
(@tbl-why-kinds).

| Kind | Held fixed | Allowed to vary | Example | Nature of the problem |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Methods (computational) | Data and code | Machine, operator | A colleague reruns your script on your data and gets your hazard ratio | Software engineering |
| Results (replicability) | Question and methods | The data: a new sample from the same population | A second trial at other sites finds a similar effect | Sampling |
| Inferential | The evidence: a reanalysis of the same data, or a replication | The analyst's choices and interpretation | Two teams with the same trial data disagree on whether the effect is clinically meaningful | Judgment |

: Three kinds of reproducibility [@goodman2016what]. {#tbl-why-kinds}

The kinds are progressively harder to secure. Inferential
reproducibility is the broadest: two analysts can share the data
and the code and still reach different conclusions, because they
chose different exclusions, models, or thresholds of clinical
importance, or weighed the same estimate against different prior
evidence. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and
Medicine (NASEM) report on the subject [@nasem2019reproducibility]
uses a simpler vocabulary for the first two rows: *reproducibility*
means consistent results from the same data, code, and conditions
of analysis, and *replicability* means consistent results from a
new study that collected its own data. This book uses the NASEM
words.

This book is about methods reproducibility. Without it the harder
kinds are out of reach: if you cannot reproduce your *own*
analysis, you cannot tell whether a discrepancy between yours and
a colleague's is a real disagreement or a bug.

### Exercises

1. Classify each scenario by the kind of reproducibility it tests.
   (a) A reviewer runs your compendium in a container and obtains
   your Table 2. (b) A team in another country repeats your
   home-visit trial and finds a smaller effect. (c) A second
   statistician reanalyzes your trial data with a per-protocol
   population and concludes that the intervention is not
   worthwhile.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) Methods: same data and code, different machine and operator.
(b) Results, which NASEM calls replicability: new data from a new
sample. (c) Inferential: the same evidence, analyzed under
different choices and judged by a different standard. Scenario
(c) can happen with a perfectly reproducible analysis, which is
why the distinction matters.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your reanalysis of a colleague's published data
gives a different odds ratio. Before arguing about whose model is
better, what must you establish, and why?

**Answer.** That you can reproduce *their* number from their data
and code (methods reproducibility). Until you can, the difference
may be a bug, a different version of a package, or a different
input file, and an argument about models would be an argument
about noise. Once their number is reproduced, the remaining
difference is a disagreement about choices, which is the
inferential kind and is worth having.
:::

## Reproducibility cases {#sec-why-cases}

Two cases show what an irreproducible analysis costs and what
finding its errors requires (@tbl-why-cases).

The Duke case opened this chapter. Its lesson, in Baggerly and
Coombes's own summary, is that the most common errors are simple,
such as row or column offsets, and that the simplest errors are
the common ones [@baggerly2009deriving]. The second case comes
from economics. In 2010 Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff
reported that countries with public debt above 90 percent of
gross domestic product (GDP) had sharply lower growth, and the
result was cited widely in arguments for austerity. Thomas
Herndon, a graduate student at the University of Massachusetts
Amherst, could not reproduce it for a class assignment. With the
authors' spreadsheet in hand, he and his professors found a
formula whose range omitted five countries, the selective
exclusion of available years, and an unconventional weighting of
the country averages. Corrected, average growth above the
threshold was 2.2 percent, not the published -0.1 percent
[@herndon2014does]. The spreadsheet error was the memorable part;
most of the gap came from analyst choices that were invisible
until someone had the file.

| Case | What went wrong | How it was found | What would have made it loud |
|---|---|---|---|
| Duke genomics (2006 to 2010) | Gene lists offset by one row; sensitive and resistant labels reversed | Two outside statisticians reconstructed the analysis from published data | Released code and data; an assertion that sample labels match their source |
| Reinhart and Rogoff (2010 to 2013) | A formula range omitted five countries; years excluded; unusual weighting | A graduate student asked for the spreadsheet | Code in a script rather than cell formulas; a count of the countries entering each average |

: Reproducibility cases, and the check that would have caught each
early. {#tbl-why-cases}

Cases like these led Congress to direct the National Science
Foundation to commission the NASEM report
[@nasem2019reproducibility]. Its central recommendation on
computational work is that researchers report the data, code,
and computational environment behind a published result clearly
enough for others to repeat the analysis, which is the compendium
of @sec-why-anatomy.

Both cases have the same shape. The code ran, the output looked
like a result, and the error surfaced only when an outsider
rebuilt the analysis at great cost. Neither error was caught by
care, and both could have been caught by a check that runs every
time. The book calls this idea **make silent failures loud**,
and every tool in the chapters that follow is a way of doing it.
The numbered habits that put the idea into practice are listed
in @sec-habits; later chapters cite them by number.

### Exercises

2. A data frame `growth` should contain one row per country-year
   for 20 advanced economies. Write the assertion that would have
   made the omitted-countries error loud before any average was
   computed. Test it on the planted subset below.

```{r}
#| label: why-growth-fixture
growth <- data.frame(
  country = rep(sprintf('Country %02d', 1:20), each = 3),
  year    = rep(2007:2009, times = 20)
)
subset_used <- growth[growth$country > 'Country 05', ]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-01-2
#| error: true
stopifnot(length(unique(growth$country)) == 20)
stopifnot(length(unique(subset_used$country)) == 20)
```

The first assertion passes on the full data. The second stops,
because the subset holds only 15 countries: the five that sort
first are missing, exactly as a spreadsheet range that starts too
low would drop them. The count is a structural check, and it
catches only what it counts; it would not have caught the
weighting choice, which is a matter of judgment for the methods
section.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In both cases the error was found by someone outside
the team. Why is that the expensive way to find it?

**Answer.** Because an outsider has to reconstruct the analysis
before checking it, and without code and data the reconstruction
is most of the work: months in the Duke case. By the time the
error surfaces, results have been published, cited, and in the
Duke case used to treat patients. A check inside the analysis
runs on every build, at no marginal cost, before anything leaves
the team.
:::

## The anatomy of a reproducible analysis {#sec-why-anatomy}

Three things must travel together for an analysis to be
methods-reproducible, shown in @fig-repro-legs. If any one of the
three is missing, the analysis cannot be rerun, and the whole
edifice falls in the manner of a stool missing a leg.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-repro-legs
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart with a single node, reproducible analysis,
%%|   branching to three requirements: Code, meaning every step is
%%|   executable; Data, meaning raw inputs are versioned; and
%%|   Environment, meaning packages, R version and operating system
%%|   are pinned."
%%| fig-cap: "The three ingredients of a methods-reproducible analysis.
%%|   Each is necessary, and each has a characteristic failure mode: code
%%|   with undocumented manual steps, data that is 'the file a colleague
%%|   emailed me', and an environment that only 'works on my machine'."
flowchart TD
  R["Reproducible<br/>analysis"] --> C["Code<br/><i>every step<br/>executable</i>"]
  R --> D["Data<br/><i>raw inputs,<br/>versioned</i>"]
  R --> E["Environment<br/><i>packages, R<br/>version, OS</i>"]
```

**Code.** Every step from raw input to final output, as
executable code. No 'I opened the file in Excel and sorted by
date.' No 'I copied the column to a new sheet.' Every
transformation must be in the script.

**Data.** Either the actual data, or a precise description of how
to obtain it. For protected health data, the description includes
the access procedure (a data-use agreement, an institutional
review board approval, a specific download location). For public
data, include the data.

**Environment.** The R version, every package version, the
operating system (OS), and system dependencies such as LaTeX or
GDAL (the Geospatial Data Abstraction Library). Without this, the
same code on the same data on a different machine can produce
different results.

| Missing leg | What you have | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Data | Code and environment | The analysis cannot run |
| Code | Data and environment | Nobody can tell what was done |
| Environment | Code and data | It works on your machine, and differs or fails on others |

: What breaks without each leg of the stool. {#tbl-why-legs}

The minimum reproducible compendium [@marwick2018packaging] is
exactly this: a directory containing code, data, and a declared
environment, structured as an R package or similar artifact
(@sec-rrtools).

### Where judgment enters

Tools such as `renv`, Docker, and Quarto make the software part
of reproducibility easy. Reproducibility is a workflow problem
disguised as a software problem, and the workflow part (which
steps to script, what counts as a data file, when to commit) is
where your judgment matters.

- **What goes in the script, and what goes in the README.**
  `library(dplyr)` belongs in the script. 'Download the file from
  the secure portal' belongs in the README. The boundary is
  whether the step can be automated; if it cannot, document it.
- **Which decisions to record.** When you exclude observations
  with systolic blood pressure above 250 mmHg as implausible, the
  decision belongs in the script as a filter, with the threshold
  and a comment saying why. 'Remove implausible BP values' without
  a threshold is not reproducible.
- **When to break the chain deliberately.** Some steps are
  irreducibly manual: results from a web tool, images labeled by
  hand, a table transcribed from a paper. Document them in the
  README and treat their output as raw input to the reproducible
  chain. Do not pretend they were automated.

These judgments are what distinguish a research compendium from a
directory of scripts.

### Exercises

3. For each item, name the leg it belongs to and where you would
   record it: (a) you removed three participants whose consent was
   withdrawn; (b) the data arrive from a secure portal after a
   data-use agreement is signed; (c) the report needs a LaTeX
   installation; (d) the analysis used `survival` 3.7-0.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
| Item | Leg | Where it is recorded |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Consent withdrawals | Code | A filter in the script on a documented list of IDs, never a hand edit of the file |
| (b) Secure portal | Data | The README: the access procedure, the agreement, the file names and checksums |
| (c) LaTeX | Environment | The Dockerfile (@sec-docker) |
| (d) `survival` version | Environment | `renv.lock` (@sec-renv) |

Item (a) is the one most often done by hand. The list of
withdrawn IDs is itself raw input; the removal is code.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague sends a script and a lockfile and says
the data are 'on the shared drive'. Which leg is missing, and what
is the symptom when someone tries to rerun it in a year?

**Answer.** Data. A path on a shared drive is not a description of
how to obtain the data: the file may have been overwritten, moved,
or edited in place. The symptom is either an error (the file is
gone) or, worse, a different number from a file with the same
name and different contents. A checksum recorded beside the
access procedure distinguishes the two.
:::

## How analyses fail {#sec-why-failures}

The failures that make an analysis irreproducible are almost
never fraud, and rarely even carelessness in any sense the analyst
would recognize at the time. They are entropy. A package was
updated between the analysis and the revision. A file was
renamed. A step was done by hand on a Thursday afternoon and
never written down, because on that Thursday it was obvious. Each
is individually trivial and individually invisible; their
accumulation is what makes an analysis irreproducible six months
later, usually to the surprise of the person who wrote it. The
remedy is not vigilance, which does not scale and cannot be
audited, but a small number of structural habits that make the
entropy impossible rather than merely discouraged.

@tbl-why-failures lists the common failures, each with the check
that makes it loud and the chapter that teaches the tool.

| Failure | How it shows up | What makes it loud | Taught in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Missing random seed | A bootstrap interval, imputation, or simulation differs on every run, usually in a late decimal place | `set.seed()` in the script; two runs compared with `identical()` | This chapter |
| Unpinned package versions | The same code returns a different number after an upgrade, perhaps with a deprecation warning nobody reads | A lockfile and `renv::status()` | @sec-renv |
| Undocumented manual steps | The reported numbers cannot be regenerated from the raw data | A script for every step; raw data kept read-only | @sec-rrtools, @sec-acquisition |
| Hidden global state | The script runs only in your session, which holds objects or options it silently uses | A fresh session for every run (`Rscript`, or a render in a clean process) | @sec-workstation |
| 'Works on my machine' | A system library, font, or LaTeX version exists on your machine and not on others' | A container that pins everything beneath R | @sec-docker |
| Stale intermediate | A figure is built from a file that was never rebuilt after the cleaning script changed | A dependency graph that rebuilds what is out of date | @sec-targets |

: Common reproducibility failures, the check that makes each loud,
and where the book teaches it. {#tbl-why-failures}

Hidden global state deserves a warning of its own, because the
default settings of the most common editor produce it.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A restored workspace hides missing code.** RStudio restores
`.RData` into every new session by default, so an object you
created by hand last month is still there, and a script that uses
it runs without complaint. On anyone else's machine, or in a
fresh session, it fails, or finds a different object of the same
name. Turn off workspace restoring in the global options, and run
the analysis with `Rscript` before you believe it works.
:::

### Worked example: break it, then fix it

The first row of the table is the easiest to see. The function
below computes a bootstrap 95 percent confidence interval for mean
ejection fraction in the book's running study, the HF-HOME trial,
and runs it twice.

```{r}
#| label: why-break-it
baseline <- read.csv(
  file.path('..', 'data', 'raw_data', 'hfhome', 'baseline.csv'),
  colClasses = c(patient_id = 'character')
)
ef <- baseline$ef_pct[!is.na(baseline$ef_pct)]

boot_ci <- function(x, reps = 2000) {
  means <- replicate(reps, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
  quantile(means, c(0.025, 0.975))
}

run_1 <- boot_ci(ef)
run_2 <- boot_ci(ef)
round(rbind(run_1, run_2), 2)
identical(run_1, run_2)
```

Nothing failed. Both intervals are plausible, and they differ only
in a late decimal place (the values change each time this page is
built), which is exactly why the omission
survives: the analyst who reruns the script before a revision sees
a slightly different number and has no way to tell drift from a
change in the data. The fix is one line, and the check that
proves it is another.

```{r}
#| label: why-fix-it
set.seed(20260423)
run_1 <- boot_ci(ef)
set.seed(20260423)
run_2 <- boot_ci(ef)
round(rbind(run_1, run_2), 2)
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Turn 'the two runs agree' into an assertion, so that a future edit
that removes the seed stops the script instead of shifting a
number.

```{r}
#| label: why-fix-it-verify
stopifnot(identical(run_1, run_2))
```

In your own project, the stronger form of this check is to run the
whole analysis twice in fresh sessions and compare the outputs
file by file, for example with `tools::md5sum()`.
:::

The same approach scales from one function to a whole project:
run it twice, in clean sessions, and compare. That is also the
right way to use a model or a coding agent for an audit, because
running the code shows failures that reading it cannot.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
A model reading a script can only guess what will fail; an agent
that runs it in a clean session can show you.

> **Context.** `analysis/run.R` in this R project reads
> `data/raw/` and writes `output/`; the project has a `renv.lock`.
> You are a coding agent with a shell. Run only against the
> synthetic files in `data/synthetic/`.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not edit any file in the project and do not
> install packages outside the project library. Run the script
> twice with `Rscript --vanilla`, in the project's container if
> it has one.
>
> **Criteria.** Report every reproducibility failure you observe,
> classified as missing seed, unpinned version, manual step,
> hidden global state, or machine dependency, with the evidence
> for each (the error message, or the files whose checksums differ
> between the two runs) and the line responsible. If the script
> fails, stop and report; do not fix it.

*Failure mode.* A model that only reads the script flags the
obvious gaps (no seed, a hard-coded path) and misses what shows
only at run time: a file present only on your disk, an object
supplied by `.Rprofile`, a nondeterministic parallel step. An
agent told to 'make it run' may edit the script until it does,
hiding the failure it found. *Check.* Confirm with `git status`
that nothing changed, then rerun the script twice yourself and
compare the outputs with `tools::md5sum()`. Record the model, the
date, and the prompt in the project log (Habit 12); the agent
sees synthetic data only (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### Exercises

4. Audit the script below (display-only) against
   @tbl-why-failures. List each failure, the line that shows it,
   and the fix.

```r
load('~/Desktop/workspace.RData')
library(dplyr)
d <- read.csv('C:/Users/me/Downloads/hf_final_v3.csv')
d <- d |> filter(keep == 1)
boot <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(d$ef_pct, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
| Line | Failure | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hidden global state: the script depends on a saved workspace | Delete the line; create every object in code |
| 2 | Unpinned version: nothing records which `dplyr` was used | `renv::snapshot()` and commit `renv.lock` |
| 3 | Machine dependency: an absolute path on one person's computer | A path relative to the project, such as `file.path('data', 'raw', ...)` |
| 3 | Manual step: `hf_final_v3.csv` is a derived file with no script that made it | Read the raw export and derive the file in code |
| 4 | Manual step: the `keep` column was set by hand | Replace it with a filter that states the exclusion rule |
| 5 | Missing seed | `set.seed()` before the bootstrap |

The `_v3` suffix is itself evidence: two earlier versions existed,
and nothing says how they differ.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Of the six failures in @tbl-why-failures, which ones
produce an error, and which a different number?

**Answer.** Hidden global state and machine dependencies usually
produce an error on another machine (an object or a file is not
found), which is the cheap case. A missing seed, an upgraded
package, and a stale intermediate produce a different number and
no error, which is the expensive case (Habit 8). A manual step
can produce either: an error if the derived file is absent, a
wrong number if an old copy is present.
:::

## Why it is worth the cost {#sec-why-cost}

Most arguments for reproducibility are framed in terms of
scientific virtue. They work for some audiences and not others.
The selfish argument is more durable: reproducibility is for
future you, and for the PI who will need the analysis again.
@tbl-why-cost sets out three events that happen on most projects.

| Event | Without a reproducible compendium | With one |
|---|---|---|
| Six months after submission, a reviewer asks for the primary analysis with a different exclusion criterion | A week reconstructing what was done, and doubt that it matches what was submitted | Half an hour: change one filter, rebuild, compare with the tagged submission |
| You discover that a unit conversion in step 7 was wrong | You cannot tell which other results, in this or other analyses, used the same step | Fix it, rebuild, and report exactly which numbers changed |
| A new postdoc takes over the project | A month learning what was done, much of it learned wrong | They rebuild the analysis on day one and start contributing |

: The cost-benefit case, by event. {#tbl-why-cost}

The cost is highest at the start of a project, and the savings
recur at every event.

The argument now has a second, external form. Since 2023 the
National Institutes of Health (NIH) has made a Data Management and
Sharing Plan a term of its awards for research that generates
scientific data, and federal
public-access policy now reaches from publications to the data
beneath them, which moves the work of producing a reusable
dataset, runnable code, and a declared environment from
administrators to the analyst. @sec-federal takes up the specific
policies and the practices that satisfy them.

### Exercises

5. Draft a short email to a skeptical PI explaining why
   reproducibility is in the group's interest. Use two events from
   the group's own recent history, in the form of @tbl-why-cost.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A model answer has four parts. It opens with the request ('I would
like to spend two days putting the readmissions analysis into a
compendium'). It names two real events, with their cost in time
('the revision in March took me eight days, most of them spent
reconstructing the exclusions'). It states what the same event
would cost afterward ('a one-line change and a rebuild'). It ends
with what the PI must do, which is usually nothing. An email that
argues from scientific virtue, or that lists tools before
naming an event the PI remembers, has missed the audience.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A PI says the project is small and will never be
revisited. Which row of @tbl-why-cost is the strongest reply?

**Answer.** Usually the first. Almost every submitted paper is
revisited at least once, by reviewers, and the reviewer's request
arrives after the analyst has moved on to other work. The cost of
that one event, without a compendium, typically exceeds the cost
of building the compendium in the first place.
:::

## Reproducibility is not correctness {#sec-why-correctness}

A reproducible analysis can still be wrong. If your code
implements the wrong test, you will reproducibly compute the wrong
p-value. Reproducibility ensures only that running the code twice
gives the same answer, not that the answer is right.

Conversely, a correct analysis can fail reproducibility: if the
seed was not set, the bootstrap interval differs between runs, as
the worked example showed; if package versions are unpinned, a
function's output may change. The analysis is correct in the
methodological sense, but the published numbers are not exactly
recoverable.

The two qualities are independent, and both are necessary. Tools
address reproducibility; statistical training addresses
correctness. The Reinhart and Rogoff case shows both at once: the
spreadsheet error was a reproducibility failure, and the weighting
was a question of correctness that only became visible once the
analysis could be rebuilt.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** An analysis is fully reproducible: pinned
environment, executable code, versioned data, one command to
rebuild every number. It also dichotomizes a continuous outcome at
the median, which costs power and makes the effect estimate depend
on the sample. What has reproducibility bought, and what has it
not?

**Answer.** It has bought the ability to find out. It has not made
the analysis right, and nothing about the infrastructure will.

What reproducibility supplies is *legibility*. The dichotomization
is in the code, at a specific line, in a form a reviewer can point
at. In an irreproducible analysis the same decision is invisible,
described in the methods as 'patients were classified as high or
low' with no way to see the cut point or how it was chosen. The
error exists either way; only one version is auditable. It also
makes the fix cheap: changing one line and rebuilding gives the
corrected result in minutes.

The failure mode to keep in view is that a fully reproducible
pipeline produces a *reliably* wrong answer, and its polish can
read as authority. A reviewer impressed by the Docker image and
the lockfile may look less hard at the model. That is why the book
puts @sec-ethics last rather than treating the infrastructure as
the destination.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 1: the compendium is the unit.** Code, data, and
   environment travel together; any two without the third cannot
   be rerun.
2. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence; derived data are a build
   product.** Every manual step is either scripted or documented
   as raw input.
3. **Habit 8: a bug that produces a plausible number is the
   expensive kind.** Both cases in this chapter ran without error;
   write the check that makes the quiet failure loud.

## Cumulative practice

### A replication exercise

The rest of this chapter has shown you two failures from the
outside: what Baggerly and Coombes found in the Duke genomics
case, and what Herndon found in Reinhart and Rogoff's spreadsheet.
Both took months, because neither original team had made its
compendium available, and the reconstruction itself was most of
the cost. The exercise below puts you on the other side of that
cost, against a paper that at least tried to avoid it, so that the
obstacles you log are the residue left even when code and data are
public.

Choose a published paper in your own field that deposits both its
code and its data openly, as a condition of publication rather
than an informal courtesy. The surest way to find one is to pick a
venue that states this as a policy you can check: a Registered
Report in a journal whose author guidelines require open data and
code for that article type, a paper in a journal that mandates
data and code availability statements with working repository
links (not merely 'data available on request'), or an article
from a repository that itself requires deposited materials as a
condition of indexing. Verify the policy on the journal's or
repository's own page before you commit to a paper; a data
availability statement that turns out to mean 'contact the
authors' is common enough that it is worth ruling out early,
before you have invested an afternoon.

With a paper in hand, reproduce one figure or one table, not the
whole analysis. Pick one with enough numeric content that
'matches' and 'does not match' are not matters of eyeballing: a
table of coefficients, a Kaplan-Meier curve with numbers you can
read off, a bar chart with labeled values. Work only from what the
paper's own compendium provides: its code, its deposited data (or
the access procedure it documents), and its stated software
versions, in that order. Do not consult the authors, and do not
patch a failure with a guess about what they must have meant;
treat a step you cannot complete from the deposited materials as
an obstacle to log, not a gap to fill in yourself.

Keep a running log as you work, with one entry per obstacle, each
tagged four ways: which leg of @fig-repro-legs it belongs to
(code, data, or environment), the specific failure from
@tbl-why-failures it resembles if any, what you did to get past it
(or that you could not), and whether the final number you obtained
matches the paper's reported figure or table, and if not, by how
much and in which direction. An obstacle log that reads 'the
script needed `dplyr`, which was not pinned to a version; I
installed the current one and it ran' is far more useful later
than one that reads only 'had some package issues'. Finish by
classifying what you tested against @tbl-why-kinds: an exact
reproduction from the authors' own data and code is a test of
methods reproducibility, and nothing in this exercise tests
whether the finding would replicate in a new sample.

This exercise has no solution key, and that is deliberate. What
counts as success varies by paper: some published compendia let
you rebuild a figure to the pixel, and some let you get within
rounding error after fixing three unpinned versions, and some
defeat you entirely despite a stated open-data policy, which is
itself a finding worth reporting. Each of these outcomes is a
valid result of the exercise, and each should be logged with the
same care, because the obstacle log is the deliverable, not the
reproduced figure.

6. *Cumulative (uses the whole chapter).* Find a published paper
   in your field with public code and data, and try to reproduce
   one figure or table. Log every obstacle, classify each against
   @tbl-why-failures and @tbl-why-legs, and state which kind of
   reproducibility (@tbl-why-kinds) your attempt tested. Use the
   fuller framing above if you have not already chosen a paper.
7. *On your own work (no key).* Take the last analysis you wrote.
   List every piece of information that is not in the script but
   would be needed to reproduce its output, and for each say how
   you would capture it in code, the README, or the lockfile.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A good log names each obstacle concretely ('`ggplot2` 3.5 changed
the default legend position, so the figure differs'; 'the
cleaned file is supplied, the raw file is not'). Most attempts
meet at least one unpinned version and one missing manual step.
An attempt that reproduces the figure exactly from the supplied
code and data tested methods reproducibility; it says nothing
about whether the finding replicates.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Ask of any analysis | Leg | Where the answer lives |
|---|---|---|
| Does one command rebuild every number from raw data? | Code | A script or pipeline (@sec-targets) |
| Is every exclusion a filter with a stated rule? | Code | The cleaning script |
| Are the raw data present, or is the access procedure documented? | Data | `data/raw/` or the README |
| Is the raw file unchanged since receipt? | Data | A recorded checksum |
| Are R and every package version recorded? | Environment | `renv.lock` (@sec-renv) |
| Is everything beneath R pinned? | Environment | A Dockerfile (@sec-docker) |
| Is every random step seeded? | Code | `set.seed()` in the script |
| Does it run in a fresh session on another machine? | All three | `Rscript`, a container, or a colleague |

: A reproducibility checklist. {#tbl-why-cheat-sheet}

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-01}

1. A reproducible analysis is one where a collaborator given the
   same data and code can obtain identical output on their own
   machine. Replicable is stronger: it means the conclusions hold
   when the study is repeated with new data. Reproducibility is
   about the computational chain; replicability is about the
   scientific claim. Methods reproducibility is the floor the rest
   of this book is about.
2. Code, data, and the computational environment (R version,
   package versions, operating system, and any system
   dependencies). Without all three, results may differ silently
   on another machine. `renv.lock` and a Dockerfile (or Apptainer
   image) are the standard tools for capturing the environment.
3. Reproducible means the analysis can be run again and produce
   the same answer. A correct analysis uses a valid statistical
   method on appropriate data. A reproducible analysis can still
   be wrong (for example, it consistently applies the wrong test);
   a correct analysis can fail reproducibility if random seeds are
   not set or package versions are not pinned. Both qualities are
   necessary; neither implies the other.
